items.title: Ukraine races to field faster interceptors as Russia hammers its energy grid
items.originalTitle: Ukraine races to field faster interceptors as Russia hammers its energy grid
items.summary: KYIV, Ukraine — Russia is still using fast jet-powered drones to batter Ukraine’s energy facilities, bridges and other critical infrastructure at speeds beyond the reach of most of Kyiv’s drone interceptors, despite U.S. President Donald Trump’s unilateral announcement on Sunday of an energy ceasefire between the two countries. Russia began using the jets heavily in July, when their numbers jumped fivefold from the previous month.

evidenceRecords.text: KYIV, Ukraine — Russia is still using fast jet-powered drones to batter Ukraine’s energy facilities, bridges and other critical infrastructure at speeds beyond the reach of most of Kyiv’s drone interceptors, despite U.S. President Donald Trump’s unilateral announcement on Sunday of an energy ceasefire between the two countries.
Russia began using the jets heavily in July, when their numbers jumped fivefold from the previous month.

They can now reach speeds of up to 373 mph (600 km/h) — more than three times the speed of the propeller-driven Geran-2 drones they evolved from — far exceeding the top velocity of the average Ukrainian interceptor drone, air force officials told lawmakers last week.
To stop the drones, Ukraine must instead rely on F-16s, newly installed machine gun turrets that use artificial intelligence to aim and costly air-defense missiles that are in short supply globally.
“Ukraine did not strike Russian oil refining and the energy sector in general for two days after the American president announced a ceasefire in the energy sector.

But Russia did not listen to the American president,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote after jets seriously damaged a gas production facility in the northeastern Kharkiv region on Sunday night.
Russia launched 167 missiles and drones overnight Tuesday into Wednesday, including 77 jet-powered drones, which officials said struck one of Kyiv’s main power plants and left 600,000 without power.

Ukraine’s Air Force says they are beginning to field more effective countermeasures, but with Russia continuing to optimize the design of jet-powered drones to destroy critical infrastructure, the development of jets and anti-jet interceptors has become the latest neck-and-neck technology race on the battlefield.

Iran shipped Russia its first Shahed-131 and Shahed-136 drones in mid-August 2022, and Moscow rebranded them the Geran-1 and Geran-2 and was firing them at Ukrainian civilian infrastructure by that October.

Those propeller-driven drones were slow enough for Ukraine to build an economical defense around mobile fire teams and cheap interceptor drones rather than spending scarce missiles on every Shahed, and in February the interceptors accounted for more than 70% of Shahed downings over Kyiv .

items.title: Sikorsky’s Nomad 100 VTOL Drone Is Now Quad-Packed In A Container For Rapid Deployment
items.originalTitle: Sikorsky’s Nomad 100 VTOL Drone Is Now Quad-Packed In A Container For Rapid Deployment
items.summary: Sikorsky has unveiled a concept for a containerized deployment package for its Nomad 100 vertical takeoff and landing uncrewed aircraft system (VTOL UAS), combining four aircraft and their support equipment inside a single 20-foot shipping container. The company is pitching the Nomad 100 Fast Pack as a way to rapidly establish autonomous air capabilities at locations without runways or other conventional support infrastructure. The concept was unveiled on October 12 at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention in Washington, D.C., where TWZ is in attendance.

evidenceRecords.text: Sikorsky has unveiled a concept for a containerized deployment package for its Nomad 100 vertical takeoff and landing uncrewed aircraft system (VTOL UAS), combining four aircraft and their support equipment inside a single 20-foot shipping container.
The company is pitching the Nomad 100 Fast Pack as a way to rapidly establish autonomous air capabilities at locations without runways or other conventional support infrastructure.
The concept was unveiled on October 12 at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention in Washington, D.C., where TWZ is in attendance.

It comes as the U.S. military seeks to expand its inventory of uncrewed systems and distribute capabilities across more dispersed operating locations, particularly in preparation for a potential large-scale conflict with China in the Indo-Pacific.
Rendering of the Nomad 100 Fast Pack in action.

Courtesy of Sikorsky, a Lockheed Martin company Rendering courtesy of Sikorsky, a Lockheed Martin company “Military commanders are asking for capability that enables them to deploy worldwide into austere environments,” said Ramsey Bentley, director of Sikorsky Advanced Concepts, speaking at AUSA.
They want greater situational awareness, the ability to conduct targeting and deliver effects at range, and the capacity to control multiple assets simultaneously, he added.
Sikorsky screencap The Nomad 100 Fast Pack is built around a standard 20-foot ISO container housing four aircraft, mission-command equipment, communications, power systems, and sustainment supplies.
A promotional video shows the Fast Pack being transported into a combat theater by one of the company’s Black Hawk helicopters as a slung load.

Sikorsky says two Nomad 100s can be prepared for flight “out of the box” in less than 15 minutes and that the other two aircraft — stored on the upper shelf of the container — can be made available within four to six hours.
The package is designed to support runway-independent operations from locations including naval vessels, tactical vehicle staging areas, and improvised landing zones.

As we have discussed in the past , the Nomad 100 combines vertical takeoff and landing with the ability to transition to fixed-wing flight, bringing airplane-like range and endurance to a compact, runway-independent package that can operate from confined locations.

items.originalTitle: F-35C Makes First Arrested Landing Aboard A Ford Class Carrier
items.summary: A U.S. Navy F-35C has made the first arrested landing for the type aboard a Ford class aircraft carrier, with the milestone taking place aboard the future USS John F. The milestone marks a major step in testing the Navy’s stealth fighter aboard its newest carrier class, following years of challenges integrating advanced launch and recovery systems. evidenceRecords.text: The Royal Navy Type 45 Destroyers appear to have received a new C-UAS system for self protection against drones.
Images released recently by the UK MoD show HMS Dauntless (D33) sporting two mystery containers that are likely acting as interceptor drone launchers.
The Ukrainian Navy ships were closing out Exercise Lion Protector, demonstrating their ability to safely manoeuvre as a small task group in company with a major warship, played by Dauntless.

The apparent lack of new, organic sensors indicate that the interceptors must be receiving targeting data from the Type 45’s existing suite, i.e. the Sampson multi-function radar, the S1850M long-range radar on the aft mast and/or the electro optic systems.
Adapting to new threats The presence of this new system on a Type 45 destroyer shows how navies are adapting to the new challenges posed by affordable drones.
This suggests HMS Dauntless could be the first Type 45 ship to trial the capability ahead of her High North deployment.

Drone attack and swarming tactics—extensively practiced by the Royal Navy and French Navy in dedicated exercises like Sharpshooter and WildFire and based on their experience from Red Sea deployments—highlighted a critical limitation in European navies’ VLS magazine depth (48 cells for Type 45 and Horizon destroyers, 32 cells for French Air Defence FREMMs).
To address this issue, the Royal Navy started transitioning toward DragonFire lasers and C-UAS helicopter (Martlet / LMM aboard Wildcat) .

The new C-UAS system spotted on Dauntless shows that the Royal Navy continues to transform the Type 45 from a conventional air-defence vessel into a highly resilient platform capable of surviving drone saturation.

evidenceRecords.text: The Hellenic Navy is currently testing a number of Corsair autonomous unmanned surface vessels (USVs) and has submitted a Letter of Request (LOR) to the United States for the procurement of at least 30 vessels to expand its unmanned maritime capabilities.

On Tuesday, October 13, 2026, Greek Minister of National Defence Nikos Dendias attended the inauguration of the Joint Unmanned and Autonomous Maritime Systems Training Centre at the Palaskas Training Centre (KEPAL), part of the Hellenic Navy’s Naval Training Command.

Photo taken during the inauguration of the Joint Unmanned and Autonomous Maritime Systems Training Centre at the Palaskas Training Centre, showing a Corsair USV (left) and the Hellenic Navy-developed Pyrpolitis USV (right).
However, the most notable highlight was a Corsair autonomous unmanned surface vehicle (USV) developed by US company Saronic .
According to a video released by the Ministry of National Defence (screenshots below), at least two Corsair USVs are currently in Greece undergoing trials with the Hellenic Navy.
The trials involved several Fleet units, with the fleet support ships HS Perseas (A377) and possibly HS Aias (A473) serving as motherships for transporting the unmanned vessels.
The trials also demonstrated the vessel’s ability to cooperate tactically with several warships.

Operating from HS Perseas Corsair USV and HS Perseas Corsair USV and HS Aias On the deck of HS Perseas The Ministry of National Defence stated that the Corsair USVs had undergone extensive trials and had been successfully evaluated by the Hellenic Navy.

A Letter of Request (LOR) has also been submitted to the United States for the procurement of an unspecified number of vessels through the government-to-government Foreign Military Sales (FMS) programme.

“The Ranger R10-3DX gives operators an affordable, compact, and highly capable radar solution that delivers the early warning and tracking performance needed to counter evolving drone threats.” The Ranger R10-3DX incorporates AI-based target classification algorithms that help users distinguish between drones, aircraft, birds, pedestrians and vehicles, enabling faster and more informed decision-making, says the company.

items.title: LaNeve to industry: ‘We are not walking away from modernization’
items.originalTitle: LaNeve to industry: ‘We are not walking away from modernization’
items.summary: The U.S. Army’s top officer sought to reassure industry leaders that the service remains committed to modernization and autonomous systems, announcing a new name for the command charged with shaping the future force during remarks at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, D.C. Christopher LaNeve said that the Futures and Concepts Command has been redesignated as U.S. Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command, or FASCOM.

evidenceRecords.text: The U.S. Army’s top officer sought to reassure industry leaders that the service remains committed to modernization and autonomous systems, announcing a new name for the command charged with shaping the future force during remarks at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, D.C.
Christopher LaNeve said that the Futures and Concepts Command has been redesignated as U.S. Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command, or FASCOM.

The change comes as the Army aligns its weapons purchases, force structure and training around new “How the Army Fights” guidance, which was published last week and explains how the service intends to wield land power in future wars.
“We are not walking away from modernization,” LaNeve said, addressing the industry partners directly at one point in his speech.

“We are sprinting towards, it,” he said, adding “and we are doing so responsibly with a recognition that resources are not endless.” LaNeve has charged FASCOM with developing corps-level autonomous capabilities through experimentation and testing.

According to a Tuesday release, the three-star command will have “capability-based formations centered on autonomous long-range fires, protection, tanks, logistics and obstacle breaching,” and will include some of the Army’s first 390A Robotic Technicians , which were activated this month.

“This goes beyond drones,” LaNeve said in the release, “FASCOM will pioneer operational concepts that harness autonomous capabilities across all warfighting functions.” The Army has come under fire recently after shuttering its experimental drone battalion in Europe less than a year after launching the novel unit to test how such a formation could operate.

evidenceRecords.text: NASA astronaut Christina Koch stands inside Kennedy Space Center’s Vehicle Assembly Building on July 14, 2021, in front of the agency’s Space Launch System (SLS) rocket that ultimately powered the Orion spacecraft on the Artemis I mission.
Koch later served as a crew member on the Artemis II mission in 2026, and on Oct. 13, 2026, NASA announced she will serve next as the agency’s acting deputy chief engineer.

NASA/Glenn Benson NASA engineer and astronaut Christina Koch will serve as the agency’s acting deputy chief engineer beginning on Sunday, Nov. 1, following the retirement of Katherine Van Hooser, who will conclude more than 35 years of distinguished service to the agency on Wednesday, Oct. 21.
In her new role, Koch will help lead NASA’s engineering community, supporting technical oversight, mission readiness, and engineering excellence across the agency’s programs and projects.
With this appointment, Koch will transition to management astronaut status and will no longer be eligible for future spaceflight assignments.
“Christina has seen NASA engineering from both sides of the equation: developing complex systems on the ground and trusting them with her life in space,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman.

“After spending nearly a year living and working aboard the International Space Station and helping lead America back around the Moon on Artemis II this year, she brings an extraordinary combination of technical expertise, operational experience, and judgment to this role.

I am excited to see the impact she will have across NASA as we return Americans to the lunar surface, build the Moon Base, get underway on nuclear power in space, and develop the capabilities that will ultimately take us on to Mars.” “Katherine has been an extraordinary leader throughout her career, bringing technical expertise, sound judgment, and an unwavering commitment to mission success to some of NASA’s most complex engineering challenges,” said Amit Kshatriya, NASA associate administrator and chief engineer.
“Her leadership has strengthened our engineering community and helped guide the agency through critical milestones and transitions.
As Marshall’s chief engineer and, since 2023, NASA’s deputy chief engineer, Van Hooser provided critical technical leadership and oversight across the agency’s programs.

items.title: US Army taps 9 companies to build next-gen command and control software
items.originalTitle: US Army taps 9 companies to build next-gen command and control software
items.summary: The U.S. Army announced that it is awarding initial contracts to several defense technology companies to build applications for its new battlefield software. The service will pay a one-year total of $93.6 million, spread out across nine companies, to create applications for its Next Generation Command and Control, or NGC2, software. “While the Army is providing capability we can deploy today, we’re also providing a blueprint and reference point for how industry can integrate in the future with interoperability and speed,” said Brig.

evidenceRecords.text: The U.S. Army announced that it is awarding initial contracts to several defense technology companies to build applications for its new battlefield software.
The service will pay a one-year total of $93.6 million, spread out across nine companies, to create applications for its Next Generation Command and Control, or NGC2, software.

The NGC2 system, in conjunction with the applications the companies build for it, will allow information sharing that streamlines mission completion across the Army’s six warfighting functions of command and control, fires, intelligence, movement and maneuver, sustainment and protection, the service said.

“While the Army is providing capability we can deploy today, we’re also providing a blueprint and reference point for how industry can integrate in the future with interoperability and speed,” said Brig.
Gen. Shane Taylor, portfolio management executive for the Command and Control Information Network.
The NGC2 will provide a shared network for technologies, weapons, sensors, devices and applications to operate within that will increase decision-making speed on the battlefield.
The chosen companies include General Dynamics Mission Systems, Air Space Intelligence Federal, Immersive Wisdom, LMI, Mente Systems, Stilman Advanced Strategies, Onebrief, Rune Technologies and AIR.
The applications will be hosted on the common data baseline, or software foundation, that Anduril Industries, Palantir, Raft and Striveworks have built in collaboration with the Army.
The Army is currently in the process of delivering the NGC2 software to the I Corps, which commands service members in the Indo-Pacific.
The move will further test NGC2 software’s ability to host technologies and devices separated by thousands of miles, some in communication-contested environments.

The Army has spent the last year moving from the experimental phase to the fielding phase of NGC2, going from prototype development to placing software in the hands of soldiers at the 4th and 25th Infantry Divisions.

In July 2026, the Army hosted a 10-day event at Fort Irwin, California, entitled Project Convergence-Capstone 6, that asked 10,000 participants from U.S. and allied forces as well as industry partners using 90 technologies to test software for the NGC2.

items.title: Estonia weighs buying light jet aircraft to shoot down Russian jet-powered drones
items.originalTitle: Estonia weighs buying light jet aircraft to shoot down Russian jet-powered drones
items.summary: VIENNA — Estonia’s new defense minister said his country should consider buying light jet aircraft to shoot down Russia’s faster, jet-powered attack drones. Martin Herem, a retired general who took office Sept. 16, floated the idea in interviews after meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv. He told The Baltic Sentinel and the daily Postimees that Estonia should study the option, saying air-to-air weapons are the most effective counter to the drones. Herem has not committed to buying anything.

evidenceRecords.text: VIENNA — Estonia’s new defense minister said his country should consider buying light jet aircraft to shoot down Russia’s faster, jet-powered attack drones.
He told The Baltic Sentinel and the daily Postimees that Estonia should study the option, saying air-to-air weapons are the most effective counter to the drones.
Martin Herem, a retired general who took office Sept. 16, floated the idea in interviews after meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv.
Herem has not committed to buying anything.
He told The Baltic Sentinel he is also looking at computer-controlled cannons, heavy machine guns and fast, jet-powered interceptor drones.
He noted that Estonia already has pilots, air-control expertise and L-39 trainers.
The two L-39 Albatros trainers Estonia uses are leased, according to the Estonian military’s website.
Their civilian status and lease terms would complicate any move to arm them, the former head of Estonia’s air force said back in April.
The proposal responds to a threat that is growing fast.
Yuriy Ihnat, a Ukrainian air force spokesman, said Ukraine intercepted about 40% of jet-powered drones in July and 60% in August, according to Hromadske.
In the same period, the number of jet-powered drones fired at Ukraine increased from a few hundred to several thousands a month.
Ukraine’s defense ministry puts their speed at more than 400 kilometers per hour.

HD Hyundai Heavy Industries press release Marking another milestone in a decade-long defense partnership, HD Hyundai Heavy Industries (HD HHI) launched the BRP Rajah Humabon , the third of six 2,400-ton Offshore Patrol Vessels (OPVs) built for the Philippine Navy, at its primary shipyard in Ulsan on Monday.

HD Hyundai Heavy Industries press release Marking another milestone in a decade-long defense partnership, HD Hyundai Heavy Industries (HD HHI) launched the BRP Rajah Humabon , the third of six 2,400-ton Offshore Patrol Vessels (OPVs) built for the Philippine Navy, at its primary shipyard in Ulsan on Monday.
The ceremonial launching—HD HHI’s first export naval vessel launch of the year—was attended by prominent diplomatic and military leaders from both nations, including Vice Admiral Jose Ma.
Ambrosio Ezpeleta, Flag Officer in Command of the Philippine Navy; Bernadette Therese Fernandez, Philippine Ambassador to South Korea; Lieutenant General Rommel P.
Roldan, Vice Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces of the Philippines; and Won-ho Joo, President & Head of Naval & Medium Size Ships Business Unit at HD HHI.
Named after the 16th-century ruler of Cebu who played a pivotal role in early Philippine history, the Rajah Humabon is scheduled for official delivery in February 2027.
BRP Rajah Humabon launching ceremony.

Advanced Maritime Capabilities Designed to enhance maritime domain awareness and coastal defense capabilities across the Philippine archipelago, the state-of-the-art 2,400-ton vessel measures 94 meters in length and 14 meters in width.

Boltz , a London-based AI startup founded by MIT researchers, builds biomolecular models and AI agents that help scientists predict molecular structures and interactions, and design potential new medicines.
Foresight, a London-based startup, helps owners of major infrastructure projects, including hyperscale data centers, predict completion dates, mitigate risks and accelerate time to revenue.

Hiverge , a Cambridge-based AI startup founded by researchers from Google DeepMind and the University of Cambridge, builds an AI discovery engine that automatically writes and optimizes algorithms for tasks such as faster AI training and complex logistics planning.

Prima Mente , a London-based AI biology startup, focuses on building biological foundation models to decode complex diseases and identify novel therapeutic targets, starting with Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s and ALS.

Riverlane, a Cambridge-based quantum computing startup, builds real-time error correction hardware and software that work across all major qubit types, helping quantum computers become reliable enough for practical use.

items.originalTitle: US Army expands drone marketplace to 33 nations
items.summary: The U.S. Army’s online marketplace for rapid drone acquisition is expanding internationally. Representatives of Canada, Croatia, Egypt, Japan, Kuwait, Morocco, Albania and Panama signed a statement of intent to join the Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) Marketplace during a ceremony Tuesday at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, D.C. Robert Brown, president and CEO of AUSA, said that the signing brought the total number of participating nations to 33.

evidenceRecords.text: The U.S. Army’s online marketplace for rapid drone acquisition is expanding internationally.

Representatives of Canada, Croatia, Egypt, Japan, Kuwait, Morocco, Albania and Panama signed a statement of intent to join the Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) Marketplace during a ceremony Tuesday at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, D.C.
Robert Brown, president and CEO of AUSA, said that the signing brought the total number of participating nations to 33.
The marketplace was launched in March 2026 with nine European signers and continues to grow across regional allies and partners.
“With today’s signing, the marketplace is now truly a global effort,” said Brent Ingraham, assistant secretary of the Army for acquisition, logistics and technology.
More recently, the Army awarded counter-UAS contract vehicles worth $7 billion through the marketplace, Ingraham said.
The Army also operates a C-UAS Marketplace developed and operated by the Joint Interagency Task Force 401 (JIATF 401) for digital procurement of counter-drone systems.

Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle, who attended the signing ceremony, said the drone marketplace was “connecting soldiers directly with builders and removing the bureaucratic middlemen.” Telle’s comments follow a Monday address to AUSA where he touted Army efforts to streamline acquisition.
The acting secretary further emphasized that the global drone marketplace builds on the Army’s demand for open architecture systems.

Telle said the Army needs to elevate open architectures beyond the tactical systems to “the strategic level,” saying the drone marketplace is a “great step forward” in sharing tactics, techniques, procedures and equipment with partners.

Previously, the service temporarily pulled soldiers from other specialties to help with space operations.
However, the soldiers’ experience was often lost when they returned to their original branches.

“The rotational system served the U.S. Army well in the past but will not meet the demands of the future, which requires a professional and sustainable approach to training, career progression and leader development for Army Space soldiers.

The Army’s Space Operations Branch was officially established in June, bringing together the newly-created enlisted occupational specialty and functional area 40As, the Army’s Space Operations Officers.

“Our space operations soldiers bring unmatched value to the Army and joint force because of the education and training they receive to execute space integration and interdiction missions — specifically counter-SATCOM, stratospheric warfare, navigation warfare and counter-sensing,” Col.
Space systems, the Army said, help soldiers with navigation, weather, communication and early warnings.

At the 2026 AUSA Annual Meeting and Exposition, Pat Williams, the company’s chief program officer, described the “production” as “an important step in delivering next-generation capability to the Netherlands.” Compared to a standard JLTV, the DXPV has been enhanced for mobility, corrosion protection, mission systems and suspension for increased off-road performance.

The Oshkosh AUSA booth also featured other platforms like its Family of Medium Tactical Vehicle A2 Low-Velocity Air Drop, or FMTV A2 LVAD, and the hybrid electric JLTV, or simply eJLTV.
With that, Williams added that “production readiness matters,” referring to how quickly Oshkosh was able to develop the DXPV.
The Dutch MoD signed an agreement with Oshkosh for the vehicles last summer and then placed an order valued between $25 and $30 million in January.
“Because we’re building on a mature platform from an active production line, we can move from concept to prototype much faster than traditional vehicle development,” Williams said.

items.originalTitle: DroneShield announces Q4 software update for counter-drone systems
items.summary: DroneShield has announced a fourth-quarter software release designed to improve drone detection, identification, tracking and defeat capabilities across its counter-unmanned aircraft systems. The update introduces a feature that flags unfamiliar radio-frequency signals exhibiting drone-like characteristics, allowing operators to investigate potential new threats that are not yet included in DroneShield’s threat library. It also improves thermal camera classification accuracy by 44%, while fixed-wing drone identification precision increases by 18% and recall by 8%, according to the company.

It also improves thermal camera classification accuracy by 44%, while fixed-wing drone identification precision increases by 18% and recall by 8%, according to the company.
The release also enables radio-frequency sensors and compatible optical cameras to work together for passive detection and visual confirmation.
With compatible Bosch Starlight cameras, operators can direct cameras towards the source of an RF detection before locking on to and tracking a drone.

For threat mitigation, connected DroneSentry-X Mk2 units can share detections to coordinate disruption, while jamming can be focused on frequencies used by the specific drone to reduce interference with nearby systems.

DroneShield said the software is available through its Mission Ready Services subscription, enabling compatible equipment already in the field to receive capability improvements without new hardware investment.
The DroneSentry-C2 software release is scheduled to become available on 3 November 2026.

items.summary: If you’ve ever had your car start sluggishly, or not at all, on a particularly frigid winter morning, you know standard batteries do not like extreme cold. That’s why NASA researchers are working to develop a battery that could function in the brutal cold of the Moon’s South Pole, where nighttime temperatures plunge to minus 328 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 200 Celsius).

evidenceRecords.text: The project is called Solid Power for Extreme Environment Adaptability and Resilience in Space (SPEARS), and it could provide NASA with an important tool to help power humanity’s sustained presence on the Moon through the Artemis campaign.

If you’ve ever had your car start sluggishly, or not at all, on a particularly frigid winter morning, you know standard batteries do not like extreme cold.

That’s why NASA researchers are working to develop a battery that could function in the brutal cold of the Moon’s South Pole, where nighttime temperatures plunge to minus 328 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 200 Celsius).

For future lunar operations, a battery will need to work immediately when warmed up and be able to power everything from an astronaut’s emergency kit to a rover capable of exploring the Moon’s darkest craters — all without posing a fire hazard.
A team of NASA researchers is working to make all that happen.

“Batteries have become an important part of our lives here on Earth, which enable our laptops, cell phones, power tools, and even our vehicles,” said Donald Dornbusch, principal investigator for SPEARS at NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, where the project is led. “We will need them on the Moon, too, and these batteries will be required to operate reliably and safely in this harsh environment.
That’s why we’re working on this technology.”
Traditional lithium-ion batteries like those in your cell phone and laptop have a critical weakness: they rely on liquid electrolytes.
Cool a conventional battery to the Moon’s nighttime temperatures, and that liquid would freeze, potentially damaging the battery.
Heat it up too much — say, to daytime lunar temperatures of 212 F (100 C) — and it won’t work until cooled.
Expose the liquid to the vacuum of space, and it evaporates.
SPEARS batteries solve these problems by replacing the liquid electrolyte with a solid ceramic- or polymer-based material.

An adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that without warning, services had been limited for terminals travelling over 100mph overnight on Wednesday – effectively limiting Ukraine’s ability to launch drones, which use satellite internet to pilot the craft.

evidenceRecords.text: A month after President Donald Trump intervened to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea, citing a desire not to upset his “very good relationship” with North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un, the commander of Army forces on the peninsula said he’d like to go bigger – both in exercise frequency and geographic scope.

Xavier Brunson, commander of United Nations Command, Combined Forces Command, and United States Forces Korea, said lessons from Ukraine prompted interest in changing the shape and structure of exercises there.

“I think what we recognize is that largely the two big exercises every year in Korea focus on large command posts; we’ve got to move away from that,” Brunson said, in response to a question from a Korean journalist.

Speaking at the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting here Monday, Gen. Xavier Brunson, commander of United Nations Command, Combined Forces Command, and United States Forces Korea, said lessons from Ukraine prompted interest in changing the shape and structure of exercises there.

“So, what we intend to do is take advantage of the knowledge that we have of the threats that exist or that prevail in the Ukraine fight,” he continued. “We’re trying to say how might we train differently, and so [Gen. Kim Sung-min, deputy commander of the Republic of Korea–U.S. Combined Forces Command] and I talk about how we would operate in a distributed fashion.”

In light of the distributed fight and scope of battle in Ukraine, Brunson suggested a training exercise that spanned from Jeju Island to Gyeonggi Province — a distance of nearly 300 miles across nearly the full span of the Korean peninsula.

“Just imagine if we trained across the entirety of the peninsula and got ourselves in a shape where we would say, ‘You can’t utilize the things that you’ve learned in the fight in the battlefield in Ukraine on us, because we learn the same lessons and we’ve distributed ourselves in such a way that we don’t make ourselves the target,” he said.

items.summary: What does it take for an autonomous robot to be faster around a course than human drone pilots? At these dizzying speeds, humans need lightning-fast reflexes. Researchers at Delft University of Technology (the Netherlands) have developed an AI system that enables a racing drone to navigate demanding courses at extreme speed using only a single camera. evidenceRecords.text: Researchers at Delft University of Technology (the Netherlands) have developed an AI system that enables a racing drone to navigate demanding courses at extreme speed using only a single camera.
It outperformed even former world champion human drone pilots in a race.
What does it take for an autonomous robot to be faster around a course than human drone pilots?
At these dizzying speeds, humans need lightning-fast reflexes.

Now published in Science Robotics, the scientific work behind this accomplishment shows how compact, efficient neural-network-based control can achieve high-performance autonomous flight under real-world conditions.
The underlying principles could help advance a much broader class of autonomous robots, from vehicles to mobile and humanoid systems.
The TU Delft team set out to investigate how far artificial intelligence can push a drone with very limited sensors, onboard computing power and energy.
This is a challenging problem: at high speed, even a small delay in sensing or control can mean missing a gate, colliding with an obstacle or losing control and crashing.
At high speed, the drone has very little time to interpret what it sees.
A neural network identifies the racing gates in the camera images, while the onboard IMU and a model of the drone estimate its position and motion.
The system does all this without GPS or external motion tracking.

"We developed a robust way of combining what the camera sees with the drone's own motion information, allowing it to navigate the track at high speed without GPS." The system also had to cope with imperfections that occur in real flight, including camera interference and sensor saturation.
For Guido de Croon, professor at Delft University of Technology, the value of drone racing goes beyond making drones fly faster.
In the current study, we made an AI efficient enough to control a drone traveling at 100 kilometers per hour (62 miles per hour) using a single camera and a small onboard processor.

items.title: NASA’s Chandra Breaks Down ‘Treble Clef’s’ Galaxy Cluster Collision
items.originalTitle: NASA’s Chandra Breaks Down ‘Treble Clef’s’ Galaxy Cluster Collision
items.summary: Wolk Astronomers have used NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory to break down the cause of a remarkable formation of radio waves they have nicknamed the “Treble Clef” because its distinct shape strongly resembles the musical symbol. The researchers discovered the Treble Clef is likely caused by an outburst from a supermassive black hole, followed by a collision of two galaxy clusters.

evidenceRecords.text: Wolk Astronomers have used NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory to break down the cause of a remarkable formation of radio waves they have nicknamed the “Treble Clef” because its distinct shape strongly resembles the musical symbol.
The researchers discovered the Treble Clef is likely caused by an outburst from a supermassive black hole, followed by a collision of two galaxy clusters.

An explanation for the Treble Clef has been particularly difficult to find because the formation lies almost directly behind the plane of the Milky Way, meaning that stars, gas, and dust from our home galaxy largely block the view from Earth.

NASA’s Chandra and the German Extended RÖntgen Survey with an Imaging Telescope Array (eROSITA) X-ray telescope found diffuse, hot gas at the location of the Treble Clef, showing that a galaxy cluster hosts the object.
The researchers also determined the galaxy cluster is, in fact, two clusters in the process of merging.
Galaxy clusters are some of the largest structures in the universe, containing hundreds of individual galaxies and huge reservoirs of superheated gas.

This new composite image of the Treble Clef and its cluster shows the multimillion-degree gas detected in X-rays by Chandra and eROSITA in blue, with some of the Chandra data derived from a special technique the authors used to highlight important features in the Chandra data.
Radio data shown in red from the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR), a large network of radio telescopes in Europe reveals the doppelganger of the musical notation.
The final piece of the combined image comes from infrared data obtained by the United Kingdom Infrared Telescope, appearing mostly white.
The authors concluded that the Treble Clef likely formed in a two-stage process.
First, an earlier outburst from a supermassive black hole in the galaxy cluster’s center drove clouds of charged particles and magnetic fields away at close to the speed of light.
This led to a type of cosmic crescendo and initially produced bright radio waves that later faded as the particles lost energy.

items.originalTitle: How to earn the US Army’s Jungle tab in Panama — and lose 10lbs
items.summary: BASE AERONAVAL CRISTÓBAL COLÓN, Panama — Though many service members venture into the hot, humid terrain of the U.S. Army’s jungle school in Panama , not all leave with the newly authorized-for-wear Jungle tab. The Panama course, back after a decades-long hiatus, resumed in 2025 as the U.S. military shifted its focus to the Western Hemisphere. evidenceRecords.text: BASE AERONAVAL CRISTÓBAL COLÓN, Panama — Though many service members venture into the hot, humid terrain of the U.S. Army’s jungle school in Panama , not all leave with the newly authorized-for-wear Jungle tab.
The Panama course, back after a decades-long hiatus, resumed in 2025 as the U.S. military shifted its focus to the Western Hemisphere.
In August, the Army confirmed it had approved the small arch-shaped patch — emblazoned with the word “Jungle” — for service-wide wear on the left shoulder.

Those who attended the course from 1990 to 1999 at Fort Sherman, now known as Base Aeronaval Cristóbal Colón, are authorized the tab retroactively , as well as those who attended the 12-day jungle school in Oahu, Hawaii, after Fort Sherman’s closure.

The 18-day course includes classes on flora, fauna, machetes, jungle first aid, fire-starting, shelter-building, and more, but showing up and trudging through muddy terrain in crippling Panama humidity is not enough to earn the tab.
“There’s a difference between graduating the course with the tab and finishing the course,” said Lt.
Andrew Eagan, the officer in charge of the Jungle Operations Training Course in Panama, or JOTC-P.
Even if students fail one part of the curriculum, as long as their failure presents no medical or safety issues, they must finish the course.
There are then five critical tasks across the course that you have to pass in order to graduate with the tab,” Eagen said.
Combat Water Survival Assessment and 5K Early in the course, participants face physical fitness tests.

The Combat Water Survival Assessment, or CWSA, requires participants to complete a variety of survival tasks in the water, including swimming in combat gear, ditching their equipment and dropping from a meters-high diving board.
The 5-kilometer run — only 3.1 miles — has proven one of the course’s toughest obstacles for many jungle school candidates.

Researchers at Sandia National Laboratories and Luxembourg Institute of Science and Technology published a technical paper titled “Revealing New Leakage Paths in GAAFETs using Predictive First-Principles Simulations.”
“Gate-All-Around Field-Effect Transistors (GAAFETs) are emerging as successors to Fin Field-Effect Transistors (FinFETs) and are central to continued scaling at advanced semiconductor nodes.

Despite their improved electrostatic control, recent measurements show that the drain current in GAAFETs deviates strongly from thermionic behavior at negative gate voltages, increasing as the gate voltage becomes more negative.
This leakage has been attributed to direct gate-drain tunneling through the high-k dielectric, enhanced by drain-induced dielectric barrier lowering (DIDBL).

Here, we use predictive, charge-self-consistent Non-Equilibrium Green Function (NEGF) simulations based on the Contact Block Reduction (CBR) method to spatially resolve this leakage pathway in GAAFETs.”
Find the technical paper here.

items.summary: BAE Systems unveiled new layered air-defense systems designed to counter missiles and drones on Monday at the annual meeting of the Association of the United States Army. The international defense company introduced the Multi-Domain Artillery Cannon System, or MDACS, and the High-Power Microwave, or HPM, as complementary systems for protecting critical installations and field units.

evidenceRecords.text: BAE Systems unveiled new layered air-defense systems designed to counter missiles and drones on Monday at the annual meeting of the Association of the United States Army.

The international defense company introduced the Multi-Domain Artillery Cannon System, or MDACS, and the High-Power Microwave, or HPM, as complementary systems for protecting critical installations and field units.

Travis Langer, BAE Systems’ communication manager, explained to Military Times that the systems together fill a capability gap created by evolving technological threats and the military’s traditional procurement process.

“Both products complement existing air defense systems, but each offer a more cost-effective solution for defense against high-volume, low-cost threats allowing the preservation of high-value missiles for the most critical targets, which extends the life and effectiveness of the entire missile stockpile,” Langer said.

The Multi-Domain Artillery Cannon System According to BAE Systems, MDACS forms the kinetic layer of the defensive shield, using precision-guided munitions called Hypervelocity Projectiles, or HVPs, for both offensive and defensive operations.

“It fills a gap that traditional artillery cannot, providing a scalable layer of protection that complements existing high-tier systems,” Langer said, adding that it allows the Defense Department “to maintain a sustainable defense without draining the budget on every single engagement.” He explained MDACS combines high-accuracy guidance with the extreme velocity of the HVP.
BAE Systems secured an Army agreement to develop a prototype of MDACS in January 2025, according to reports .
The High-Power Microwave BAE Systems describes its HPM system as a “scalable directed energy weapon” built with an emphasis on affordability.
Although the system remains in the prototype stage, BAE Systems said it has reached Technology Readiness Level 6, or TRL 6.
Layered air-defense Langer explained that the two systems are not specifically designed to be used together, but they could complement each other if the mission set requires it.

evidenceRecords.text: The Army awarded Anduril Industries a contract on Sept. 30 worth up to $1.8 billion over five years to help the service transition its new battlefield software from the experimentation phase to the fielding phase.

Anduril previously helped develop the prototype for the service’s Next Generation Command and Control, or NGC2, for the 4th Infantry Division, using its proprietary AI-powered operating system Lattice.

“A common data layer allows the Army to integrate new systems without rebuilding the underlying architecture for every sensor, application, or weapon, so new capabilities can be fielded on the same foundation as those already in use,” Anduril said.

The Army awarded $162.8 million to Anduril to continue working on NGC2’s common data baseline, or software foundation, as it begins to implement it across the service’s I Corps, which commands service members across the Indo-Pacific.
The contract contains options that can grow its value up to $1.8 billion.
Anduril, along with Palantir, Raft and Striveworks, have helped build out the baseline.
The NGC2 system will allow technologies, weapons, sensors, devices and applications from across the force to operate on the same network and increase decision-making speed on the battlefield.

By expanding the NGC2 system to the I Corps, technologies will have to figure out ways to connect to the same network despite being separated by thousands of miles and experiencing interrupted or degraded connectivity.
This will provide the Army and Anduril an opportunity to test how well information flows between the systems as they access the NGC2 framework in a myriad of environments.

During a July 2026 ten-day event at Fort Irwin, California, entitled Project Convergence-Capstone 6 , the Army asked 10,000 participants from U.S. and allied forces, as well as industry partners using 90 technologies to test software for the NGC2.
Afterward, the Army awarded a contract to Anduril to develop the software prototype for NGC2 for the 4th Infantry Division.
Over the past year, Anduril has conducted several operational exercises in collaboration with the Army to test the NGC2’s common data layer baseline.

evidenceRecords.text: Researchers at ETH Zürich and New York University published a technical paper titled “Understanding the Power Consumption of Modern High Bandwidth Memory: Experimental Analysis and Modeling Using Real HBM2 DRAM Chips.” Abstract Excerpt: “We perform the first comprehensive experimental characterization of power consumed by real HBM2 DRAM chips.

Our extensive characterization yields 1) the empirical basis for developing new, accurate HBM power models or validating existing power models and 2) key insights into structural and data-pattern-dependent variation of power in HBM2 chips.

Out of our 13 new findings and 6 key takeaway messages, we highlight: 1) a read operation consumes significantly higher current than any other operation and 2) the toggled data bus signals in a data transfer burst significantly affect current draw where toggling all HBM2-internal bank group bus signals causes 29.4% higher power consumption than keeping them constant.

Leveraging our empirical insights into HBM2 power consumption, we engineer an access pattern that yields 23.6% higher power consumption on average across 36 tested HBM2 chips than the highest-power-consuming JEDEC-specified current measurement loop.” Find the technical paper here .

evidenceRecords.text: WARSAW — With Poland only partway through an air defense modernization effort, the Polish Air Force has been operating at the highest readiness on a nightly basis, which is putting heavy strain on personnel and equipment, according to Maj.
Gen. Ireneusz Nowak, the operational commander for the Polish Armed Forces.
Nowak said 80 percent of his service’s attention is focused on air defense, with the ground and air components of Poland’s integrated air defenses still three to four years away.
In the meantime, the Air Force has changed how it operates in order to fill the gap.
Starting Oct. 1, the service stopped following Visual Identification (VID) procedures in which a pilot confirms a target’s type, markings or nationality by sight before engaging.
“So now we are much more flexible, much more responsive,” Nowak, who is responsible for Polish airspace, said.

During the panel discussion, Nowak acknowledged that using fighter jets to shoot down cheap drones is a bad cost ratio for Poland, but said there simply isn’t any other option at the moment. “We need to develop massive, responsive weapons systems capable to counter-react the UAVs operations,” he said.
Poland should have some options, but systems that the country hoped to have ready now are still underway.
Nowak pointed to the integration of Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System missiles on F-16s as a near-term solution, but said there is a hitch in getting those weapons in the field.

“It hasn’t happened yet, and we are trying to process it, but we [Polish Air Force] couldn’t get the fuses, which were utilized by the US Air Force, and were certified, because of business restrictions and limitations.
So we are waiting for the new type of the fuse,” he concluded.

Nowak also mentioned the possibility of using the F/A-50GF aircraft to combat drones, which Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz announced earlier this month has officially commenced combat duty.

evidenceRecords.text: Despite massive technological shifts, that paradigm still holds, which is why the U.S. Army and Navy have teamed up to keep systems operational — even in the extreme cold of the Arctic .

The team focused on different configurations of thermal wrappings, insulation and other components to ensure that parts of the kit’s components that are particularly vulnerable to cracking and freezing — hoses, valves, bladders and pumps — were able to withstand the greater threshold for cold, according to a recent Army release.

“Our armed forces live and operate in extremely cold and difficult conditions, so having these facilities operational is important for their physical and mental health while serving in the Arctic and other high-north environments,” said Dr. Dan Tague, a research chemist at CRREL, one of seven U.S. Army Engineer Research and Development Center laboratories.
Despite massive technological shifts, that paradigm still holds, which is why the U.S. Army and Navy have teamed up to keep systems operational — even in the extreme cold of the Arctic.
As the Department of Defense eyes greater operability in the far north, these low temperatures can wreak havoc on equipment and machinery (and toilets), with ice becoming enemy No. 1.

Which is why the Naval Facilities Engineering and Expeditionary Warfare Center, or NAVFAC EXWC, and the Cold Regions Research and Engineering Laboratory, or CRREL, began working with both branches to field a rapidly deployable Triple Container rigid-wall shelter system usable in temperatures as low as -50 degrees Fahrenheit.
The already fielded version can operate in temperatures as low as -15 degrees Fahrenheit.
The result, per the release, far exceeded the objectives, with the TRICON-based system staying operational down to -65 degrees Fahrenheit.
Testing took place in CRREL’s New Hampshire-based Extreme Cold Chamber, a 288-square-foot cold room capable of reaching temperatures as low as -90 degrees Fahrenheit, per the release.

While military units typically have to wait until the Alaskan winter reaches its peak to simulate similar conditions, the controlled environment allowed the research team to create conditions similar to those of the real world.

items.summary: Nearly all U.S. soldiers completed a mandatory test meant to track the effects of blast exposure and monitor brain health across the Army, the service said in a release . evidenceRecords.text: Nearly all U.S. soldiers completed a mandatory test meant to track the effects of blast exposure and monitor brain health across the Army, the service said in a release .
The test, or Neurocognitive Assessment Tool, is computer-based and records neurological activity, such as attention, concentration, reaction time, memory, processing speed and decision-making.
Testing started in 2024 in response to reports about the effects that routine weapons training can have on the brain, including traumatic brain injury.

Active-duty, National Guard and Reserve soldiers in high-risk military occupational specialties, including combat engineers and explosive ordnance technicians, as well as troops operating heavy weapons systems, must take the assessment every year, starting soon after they enlist.
All other soldiers are required to test every three years.
Medical professionals use the data to monitor service members’ cognitive health throughout their military careers, allowing them to spot significant changes, including potential brain injuries.

“[The NCAT] is an important part of taking care of soldiers, but what this does is, it sets a baseline for reaction times and for memory,” Jordan Gillis, assistant secretary of the Army for installations, energy and environment, said in a release.

“By establishing a baseline for all soldiers, we’re able to monitor brain health, as well as … let medical providers help with treatment, if required.” According to the Sept. 30 release, the Army is expected to publish a directive about the Neurocognitive Assessment Tool and a broader overpressure program, which includes hazard assessment, exposure tracking, risk mitigation, cognitive monitoring, information management, illness and injury reporting and training and education.
“The takeaway is we are trying to take care of soldiers and monitor their health,” Gillis said.

“And if there is an impact, we’ll be able to treat them.” Reaching the milestone of 97% of soldiers being tested on the NCAT “demonstrates our commitment to cognitive safety, medical readiness and warfighting capability,” Gillis added.

The announcement of the milestone came just one month after the Government Accountability Office released the findings of its investigation into the ability of military services to provide the baseline cognitive assessments.

As robots move beyond warehouses and other controlled environments and into everyday life, solving these navigation challenges will be critical to achieving broad consumer acceptance and large-scale deployment.

At RoboBusiness 2026, Aaron Edsinger, the co-founder and CEO of Hello Robot , and Matt Anderson, the co-founder and CEO of A&K Robotics , will take part in the session, “Shared Spaces: Navigating Challenges for Indoor Robots.” RoboBusiness will be on Oct. 20 and 21 in Santa Clara, Calif.
Edsinger and Anderson will give their talk at 3:30 p.m.
Meet the speakers Aaron Edsinger is co-founder and CEO of Hello Robot, which developing practical, safe, and accessible robots for people.
With a passion for building robots and robot companies, he has founded four companies focused on bringing human collaborative robots to the consumer, manufacturing, healthcare and research markets.

As robotics director at Google, Edsinger led the business, product and technical development of two of Google’s central investments in robotics, and worked closely with senior vice president and C-level executives to define the overall robotics strategy.
Edsinger is a recognized robotics innovator with a broad understanding of the entire robot product design stack, including human–robot interaction, UX design, and mechanical design.
Matt Anderson is co-founder and CEO of A&K Robotics, which is building autonomous mobility infrastructure for complex, human-centered environments such as airports.

He leads the company’s product strategy, which includes Cruz, a self-driving mobility robot that carries passengers through high-traffic, dynamic environments such as airport terminals, and Kineos AI, a platform for socially intelligent autonomy that enables systems to move naturally through dynamic spaces.
Anderson brings credibility with enterprise and public-sector partners by translating advanced autonomy into institution-ready solutions.

The model fills a growing gap as general-purpose frontier models lock down their cyber capabilities, blocking defenders in the process.
The article AI guardrails designed to stop hackers are now blocking defenders, and Orion-1 aims to fill the gap appeared first on The Decoder .
Artemis Security has launched Orion-1, an AI model that investigates and responds to cyberattacks on corporate networks on its own.
It connects scattered log data from networks, endpoints, and cloud services to trace attacks back to a single actor and kick off countermeasures.
On the company's own benchmark, Orion-1 outperforms general-purpose models like Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol, with the biggest gap in attack reconstruction at 80.8 versus 58.3 points.
General-purpose AI models are becoming a growing problem for security teams, since the same skills also help attackers.
Artemis Security wants to close that gap with a purpose-built model.

US startup Artemis Security has launched Orion-1, a model designed to investigate and respond to attacks on corporate networks on its own, beating Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol on the company's own benchmark.

Orion-1 processes log data from auth services, cloud setups, corporate endpoints, SaaS apps, and network gear, then connects individual signals like a corporate account login, new cloud permissions, and a freshly created email inbox rule to tie them back to a single attacker.

Artemis fine-tuned Orion-1 on tasks drawn from its own security operations, including spotting suspicious patterns in log data, hunting for known attack techniques, writing new detection rules, and containing live attacks.
Artemis calls Orion-1 a "Frontier Foundation Model" but only describes this fine-tuning in its blog post, and it's unclear whether the company built on top of an existing model from another provider.
Artemis reports results across five tasks and tested Grok 4.7 and Kimi K3 alongside Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol.
The biggest gap shows up in attack reconstruction, where Orion-1 scored 80.8 compared to 58.3 for the next-best model.
Orion-1 is live in a private preview for select customers on the Artemis platform, where customers set limits per action type on how much the model can decide on its own.

Lisa Yang Integrative Computational Neuroscience (ICoN) Center argue that a crucial metric for the biological plausibility of an artificial neural network’s approach to learning is the network’s ability to organize itself, without the guiding hand of a developer.

evidenceRecords.text: Artificial neural networks can learn to recognize images, use language, or write computer code.
Like the brain’s circuits, they reorganize themselves as they learn, adjusting the strengths of their connections to improve their performance.

Lisa Yang Integrative Computational Neuroscience (ICoN) Center argue that a crucial metric for the biological plausibility of an artificial neural network’s approach to learning is the network’s ability to organize itself, without the guiding hand of a developer.
They show that it is possible for an artificial neural network to build its own learning machinery.

“That’s not achievable by just designing a circuit that works very well.” An artificial neural network’s value to neuroscience should instead be judged by the extent to which it can organize itself — not just its connections, but also the machinery that adjusts those connections.

“If the synaptic motifs we propose are, in fact, used by the brain to do what backpropagation does for artificial neural networks, then we will have a strong connection at the level of fundamental mechanisms between artificial and natural networks — between machines and brains,” he says.

items.title: Can AI understand space, time and pain?
items.originalTitle: Can AI understand space, time and pain?
items.summary: Artificial intelligence can do remarkable things, but how much does it actually understand about the world? Researchers have found that surprisingly specific information can be extracted from the inner workings of large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT. Using mathematical tools to probe a model's internal activity, they can identify where a city is located on a map, when a historical figure lived or what emotion a character feels, even detecting descriptions of pain. Many have interpreted these findings as evidence that AI models build an internal picture of the world.

evidenceRecords.text: Artificial intelligence can do remarkable things, but how much does it actually understand about the world?
Researchers have found that surprisingly specific information can be extracted from the inner workings of large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT.

Using mathematical tools to probe a model's internal activity, they can identify where a city is located on a map, when a historical figure lived or what emotion a character feels, even detecting descriptions of pain.
Many have interpreted these findings as evidence that AI models build an internal picture of the world.
Some have even linked them to debates about whether AI might have the capacity to suffer.
These questions have taken on new urgency as debate grows over whether AI systems could suffer or warrant moral consideration, prompting some companies to restrict harsh treatment of their chatbots.
But a new paper by Elan Barenholtz, Ph.D., of Florida Atlantic University suggests that the evidence may be weaker than it appears.
The paper, "World Properties Without World Models: Distributional Associations and the Interpretation of Decoding Results from Language Models," is available as a preprint on arXiv.
It examines whether the same information attributed to language models can be extracted from much simpler mathematical structures called word vectors.
These vectors capture patterns in which words tend to appear together, without accounting for context.
Barenholtz found that they can reveal much of the same information as LLMs.

"This suggests that being able to read something out of an AI system doesn't prove the system actually has a kind of internal model of those things," said Barenholtz, an associate professor of psychology in FAU's Charles E.

evidenceRecords.text: New restrictions on the speed at which some of Ukraine's weapons can travel and stay connected to the Starlink internet network have disrupted Ukraine's battlefield "missions", President Volodymyr Zelensky's adviser has warned.
Serhiy Beskrestnov said Ukraine had not been told about speed limits set overnight at 100mph (160km/h) by Elon Musk's SpaceX company.
Beskrestnov said SpaceX's move "cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation".
The firm has not commented.

In Wednesday's post on Telegram, Beskrestnov said that SpaceX had "implemented overnight a speed limit on Starlink terminals" and this had already resulted in "the disruption of a number of missions".
In a follow-up post, the adviser stressed that Starlink was the most effective tool for enabling interceptors to shoot down Russia's newly developed jet-propelled drones.
It comes as at least 600,000 people across Ukraine were left without electricity after deadly overnight Russian missile and drone strikes, Zelensky said.
Pictures from Kyiv showed residents, some dressed in their pajamas, with bloodied faces.

He added that "critical" energy infrastructure had been hit in Kyiv and the capital region, and in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv – despite US President Donald Trump's claim on Sunday that an "energy ceasefire" was in place between Russia and Ukraine.

items.summary: WARSAW — The European Commission will continue to strengthen its defense capabilities to help defend Ukraine in its ongoing conflict with Russia, according to Commissioner for Defence and Space Andrius Kubillius. “It’s very crucial to help Ukraine to defend itself and to defend the whole Europe,” Kubilius said here at the Warsaw Security Forum on Tuesday. Kubillius’ comments come after the Trump administration has repeatedly called for Europe to become more self-reliant.

evidenceRecords.text: WARSAW — The European Commission will continue to strengthen its defense capabilities to help defend Ukraine in its ongoing conflict with Russia, according to Commissioner for Defence and Space Andrius Kubillius.
“It’s very crucial to help Ukraine to defend itself and to defend the whole Europe,” Kubilius said here at the Warsaw Security Forum on Tuesday.
Kubillius’ comments come after the Trump administration has repeatedly called for Europe to become more self-reliant.
However, Kubillius said his remarks are unrelated to US President Donald Trump’s statements alone, but rather a shift in global defense posturing as a whole.

“And that’s why [the] Commission president proposed to look into possibility to have what is called now the European Security Council, with member states, and … [the] United Kingdom, Ukraine, Norway, and Canada, which is close to Europe,” Kubilius said.

During her annual State of the Union Address in September, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen pushed for the creation of the European Security Council, as Breaking Defense previously reported.
The European Security Council could address the hurdle of fragmentation across the continent, Kibillius explained Tuesday.
Norwegian Minister of Defense Tore O.
Sandvik agreed at the Warsaw Security Forum that Europe as a whole needs to band together.
“We now have a coalition of 11 countries in Europe supporting the anti-ballistic coalition, trying to develop anti-ballistic missile systems for Europe, because we need that,” Sandvik said.
“To a global level, we can support both countries in the Middle East, the US themselves, Europe, and our Pacific friends.
What we can do in Ukraine, we can pass, we can develop, we can learn, and we can build new systems,” he added.

evidenceRecords.text: Artificial neural networks can learn to recognize images, use language or write computer code.
As artificial intelligence becomes more powerful, its ability to handle humanlike tasks is undeniable.
Like the brain's circuits, they reorganize themselves as they learn, adjusting the strengths of their connections to improve their performance.
In a paper published in PNAS, scientists at MIT's McGovern Institute for Brain Research and the K.

Lisa Yang Integrative Computational Neuroscience (ICoN) Center argue that a crucial metric for the biological plausibility of an artificial neural network's approach to learning is the network's ability to organize itself, without the guiding hand of a developer.
They show that it is possible for an artificial neural network to build its own learning machinery.

With some simple instructions about how and when connections should change, a group of randomly connected units can reshape itself into an effective information-processing network, learning from the data it is trained on.
"Current AI technology is working very well, but it doesn't necessarily use a learning algorithm that is used by the brain," says Qianli Liao, a K.

Lisa Yang ICoN Center postdoctoral fellow in the labs of MIT professors and McGovern Institute members Tomaso Poggio and Mark Harnett, and co-first author of the PNAS paper with MIT research scientist Liu Ziyin and graduate student Yulu Gan.
Liao explains that engineers design the rules about how connections change as an artificial neural network processes training data and receives feedback about its mistakes.

"None of these can work without knowing the rules behind neuron-neuron interactions," he says. "That's not achievable by just designing a circuit that works very well." An artificial neural network's value to neuroscience should instead be judged by the extent to which it can organize itself—not just its connections, but also the machinery that adjusts those connections.

"If the synaptic motifs we propose are, in fact, used by the brain to do what backpropagation does for artificial neural networks, then we will have a strong connection at the level of fundamental mechanisms between artificial and natural networks—between machines and brains," he says.

"That's not achievable by just designing a circuit that works very well." An artificial neural network's value to neuroscience should instead be judged by the extent to which it can organize itself—not just its connections, but also the machinery that adjusts those connections.

evidenceRecords.text: ElliQ extracts memories from every conversation with the user and classifies them based on importance and relevance, injecting context into future conversations. | Source: Intuition Robotics The New York State Office for the Aging, or NYSOFA, last week extended its partnership with Intuition Robotics.
The company will continue bringing its ElliQ AI companion to aging New Yorkers at risk of loneliness and social isolation.
With the expansion, NYSOFA and Intuition Robotics created a new three-year, $2.1 million agreement.
The expansion builds on the organizations’ three years of experience working together.
During that time, ElliQ has demonstrated its ability to reduce loneliness and improve health and wellbeing.
The robot also helps older adults remain healthier and more independent in their own homes.

“Loneliness and isolation are commonly heard today, but make no mistake, the health effects are devastating, and NYSOFA is working continuously to provide the help older New Yorkers need,” said Greg Olsen, director of the office .

“ElliQ is an essential tool to help combat the loneliness epidemic, joining dozens of other projects launched by NYSOFA to overcome the digital divide, address social isolation, improve health and wellness, and support caregivers.” NYSOFA established its first public-private partnership in 2018, following a report by AARP and the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) on the impact of loneliness and social isolation on older adults and Medicare spending.
It stated that loneliness and isolation are equivalent to smoking almost a pack of cigarettes per day, cost Medicare more than $7 billion to treat, and make chronic conditions worse.
In addition to its partnership with NYSOFA, Intuition Robotics has similar partnerships in Wisconsin, Florida, and Washington.
In Washington, the program is aimed at Medicaid recipients .

“This partnership extension continues our long term partnership with the state of New York, and its Office for the Aging, reflecting three years of measurable, record-breaking engagement results: older adults across New York are engaging with ElliQ more often, feeling less lonely, and staying more connected to the people who matter to them,” said Dor Skuler, co-founder and CEO of Intuition Robotics.

items.title: HiRO-ACEv2: Simulating extreme weather at 3 km resolution for a fraction of the cost
items.originalTitle: HiRO-ACEv2: Simulating extreme weather at 3 km resolution for a fraction of the cost
items.summary: We introduce HiRO-ACEv2, the newest update to our High Resolution Output Ai2 Climate Emulator (HiRO-ACE) system. HiROv2 can reproduce even extremely rare rain, wind, and pressure events with high accuracy, while the full system can generate global 3 km climate data at about 1/300th the cost of X-SHiELD, a high-resolution global atmospheric model that explicitly simulates storms and other small-scale weather.

evidenceRecords.text: We introduce HiRO-ACEv2, the newest update to our High Resolution Output Ai2 Climate Emulator (HiRO-ACE) system.

HiROv2 can reproduce even extremely rare rain, wind, and pressure events with high accuracy, while the full system can generate global 3 km climate data at about 1/300th the cost of X-SHiELD, a high-resolution global atmospheric model that explicitly simulates storms and other small-scale weather.
HiRO-ACE, introduced earlier in 2026, has two parts: ACE, an AI model that operates at a coarser 100 km resolution, and HiRO, a model that sharpens those coarse outputs into fine 3 km detail.

The biggest change in HiRO-ACEv2 is the new downscaling model, HiROv2, which can now 1) predict several high-resolution fields at once instead of just rainfall, so it can capture a much wider range of extreme weather, and 2) has improved skill in predicting extreme events.
Our main focus with HiRO-ACEv2 was to simulate extreme events well.
Changes to how we train HiROv2 improved its ability to reproduce the most intense rain, wind, and pressure values.
When given coarsened X-SHiELD data, it matches the target simulation's high-resolution statistics to within 3%, even for events so rare they occur only once in a million data points.

It also accurately estimates the total energy of tropical cyclones, including storms it never saw during training, and generates hurricanes with realistic eyes and rain bands, though winds and pressure around the eye remain somewhat more lopsided than in X-SHiELD.
We also trained an updated version of ACE for this system.
Over a 10-year simulation, its hurricanes, average climate patterns, and overall distributions of rain, wind, and pressure all line up well with X-SHiELD.
That tells us ACE's coarse simulations are a solid foundation for producing long-term high-resolution climate data.
Putting HiROv2 and ACE together, we generated a full year of global 3 km data.

evidenceRecords.text: Trump announced a new Super Intelligence task force with the White House AI czar Jay Clayton in charge of a group responsible for making sure the US leads international competition in artificial intelligence development.

"Bigger than the Industrial Revolution and the internet" — US President Donald Trump used a comparison borrowed from "many others" to describe artificial intelligence (AI) in his announcement of a "Super Intelligence Force."
The president's move to address the rapid development of the AI industry came after he met with top AI executives at the end of September — and a month before midterm elections in November.
Trump has faced intensifying pressure and warnings from business and political leaders about the mostly unregulated technology.
The name echoes Trump's September executive order renaming "Artificial Intelligence" as "Super intelligence" (SI).
Jay Clayton, the director of national security and the president's new AI czar, is the task force leader.

The task force will coordinate the government's effort "to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence," Trump said, and "will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans."
Trump has made it clear he does not want regulation to "stifle" progress in the SI industry, and a reported charter for the group says it will work to prevent "overregulation and regulatory capture."
The White House has not released any information about the Super Intelligence Force, but a copy of a charter detailing the group's responsibilities was reported in The Wall Street Journal
Clayton, whom Trump named AI czar in early October, is to chair the task force.

He told The Wall Street Journal he expected AI mechanisms to be "developed in dialogue," citing risk models the Securities and Exchange Commission, which he headed during Trump's first presidential term, and the Federal Reserve developed for the financial industry.
Key members of Trump's Cabinet, including Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, are also on the task force.
The reported charter also listed David Sacks, Trump's former AI czar, and Condoleezza Rice, former secretary of state under President George W.
, several key Republicans were not briefed on plans for the Super Intelligence Force before Trump's announcement.

evidenceRecords.text: US President Donald Trump on Wednesday said major oil, gas and mineral exploration was set to begin in Greenland.
His announcement follows a security agreement between the United States, Denmark and the Arctic island's leaders.
Trump offered no details about which companies would be involved, where exploration would take place or when operations would begin.
"Massive Oil, Gas, and Mineral Exploration is getting ready to begin in our new and beautiful Greenland!" Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
He also claimed that experts believed Greenland held some of the world's largest deposits of easily accessible oil, without providing evidence.
Greenland is believed to hold substantial untapped oil reserves, but their commercial viability remains uncertain due to high extraction costs, harsh Arctic conditions and environmental restrictions.
No commercial oil production has been established in Greenland.
Greenland has significant mineral resources, including rare earth elements used in electronics, renewable energy technologies and military equipment.
The island has also attracted interest for its potential oil and gas reserves, although exploration in the harsh Arctic environment presents considerable technical and economic challenges.
In August, reports that a US oil company was preparing operations in a remote part of eastern Greenland prompted unease among residents and local authorities.
In the same post, Trump described Greenland's strategic location as "second to none" for US and European security.

items.summary: Researchers at Columbia University, Google DeepMind , and Google published a technical paper titled “Back to the Future: Rethinking EDA Infrastructure for Agentic Systems in Chip Design Verification.” Abstract “The unprecedented computational scale of modern artificial intelligence depends on complex, multi-billion-transistor Systems-on-Chip, yet the workflows that verify these chips remain stubbornly manual.

evidenceRecords.text: Researchers at Columbia University, Google DeepMind , and Google published a technical paper titled “Back to the Future: Rethinking EDA Infrastructure for Agentic Systems in Chip Design Verification.” Abstract “The unprecedented computational scale of modern artificial intelligence depends on complex, multi-billion-transistor Systems-on-Chip, yet the workflows that verify these chips remain stubbornly manual.

Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have made rapid inroads into Electronic Design Automation (EDA), approximately 74.6% of existing studies target static Register-Transfer Level (RTL) code generation, leaving post-simulation verification and interactive waveform debugging largely untouched.

BTTF distills massive, unstructured simulation dumps into a normalized relational SQLite database and couples it with a collaborative multi-agent orchestration engine that translates natural-language verification queries into schema-aware SQL while correlating signal anomalies with versioned RTL repositories.
Across a 150-query benchmark, BTTF attains 95.33% execution accuracy, charting a practical path toward autonomous EDA verification.” Find the technical paper here .
